Finding the right PSI

Not on the tire sidewall — that's the max. Look on the sticker inside the driver's door jamb. Cold pressure only: check before driving or 3+ hours after.

The penny test

Stick Lincoln head-down into a tread groove. If you can see the top of his head, you're below 2/32 — replace now, especially before rain season.

instances.html:
Home Plumbing Cheat Sheet

Most leaks are one washer away from fixed, user_name. Here's where to start.

Before anything: shut off the water

Fixture shutoff valves sit under sinks and behind toilets. Whole-house valve is usually near the meter or where the main line enters. Turn clockwise to close. Open a faucet to drain pressure.

Clogged drain
  1. Boiling water first — clears grease
  2. Plunger with a good seal — 15–20 firm pushes
  3. Drain snake through the trap arm
  4. Skip chemical drain cleaner: it eats pipes too
Dripping faucet

Usually a worn cartridge or O-ring. Shut off supply, plug the drain so tiny parts don't vanish, and photograph each layer as you disassemble. Take the old part to the hardware store to match it.

Running toilet

Ninety percent of the time it's the flapper. Cheap, five-minute swap. Test: drop food coloring in the tank; if color shows in the bowl without flushing, the flapper is leaking.

Call a pro for: gas water heaters, anything behind a wall, sewage backups, and burst pipes. Not worth the DIY badge.

Snacks: dry, one-handed, not greasy. Pretzels, grapes, popcorn in a bowl. Save the nachos for the halftime of a movie.

Set a stopping time. Leaving at 10 with everyone happy beats leaving at 1 a.m. with grudges.

Two minutes of planning beats twenty of panic, user_name. Keep it simple.

Smoke alarms

  • Test monthly — press and hold the button
  • Replace batteries yearly; replace the whole unit every 10 years
  • Interconnected alarms wake everyone faster
Extinguishers: the PASS method
  • Pull the pin
  • Aim at the base of the fire
  • Squeeze the handle
  • Sweep side to side

Only if the fire is small, contained, and you have a clear exit behind you.

Escape plan
  • Two ways out of every room
  • Pick one outdoor meeting spot
  • Practice at night, twice a year
  • Sleep with bedroom doors closed — it slows smoke
Get out, stay out, call for help. Never go back inside — not for pets, not for photos, not for anything.

Before you speak

Home Air Filter & HVAC Cheat Sheet

Filters are cheap. Compressors are not. Here's the quick version, user_name.

Rule of thumb: check monthly, swap every 1–3 months (more often with pets, allergies, or a dusty remodel).
MERV ratings, decoded
MERVCatchesGood for
1–4Dust, lint, pollenCheap protection, basic systems
5–8Mold spores, pet danderMost homes — the sweet spot
9–12Fine dust, smokeAllergy households
13+Bacteria, virus carriersOnly if your blower can handle it

Too-high MERV starves airflow. A strained motor runs hot and dies loud.

Reading the size on the frame

It's three numbers, like 20x25x1: width × height × thickness. Nominally. Actual size is usually a hair smaller — measure before you order online.

  • Bring the old filter to the store. Easiest cheat code.
  • Arrow on the frame points toward the blower/airflow direction.
  • No arrow printed? Air flows from return duct toward the unit.
Signs it's overdue
  • Filter looks grey and fuzzy (hold it to light — can't see through? Swap).
  • Weak airflow from vents.
  • Dust settling fast on surfaces.
  • Musty smell when the fan kicks on.
Smells like burning? Shut the system off and call a tech. That's not a filter problem.
One-time vs. washable

Disposable pleated filters win on filtration. Washable/reusable ones save money but generally sit at MERV 1–4 — great if your main goal is protecting the equipment, not your sinuses.

Change it on the first of the month and you'll never wonder again.— every HVAC tech, ever

Everyday Clothing Sizing & Fit Cheat Sheet

Sizes are opinions. Measurements are facts. Trust the tape, user_name.

Measure yourself once, shop forever
  • Chest/bust: around the fullest part, tape level, arms down.
  • Natural waist: bend sideways — the crease is your waist, not your jeans' waist.
  • Hips: around the fullest part, usually 8–9" below the waist.
  • Inseam: from crotch seam to ankle bone on pants that fit.
  • Sleeve: shoulder point to wrist, slightly bent arm.

Write these in your phone notes. You'll use them more than your insurance card.

Why sizes lie

Vanity sizing creeps numbers down over time, and every brand drafts its own fit block. A medium is a suggestion. The size chart is the contract.

Brand typeTends to run
Fast fashionSmall, inconsistent
AthleticFitted, snug shoulders
Heritage/workwearBoxy, roomy
LuxuryTrim, closer to true measure
Fit checkpoints
  • Shirt: shoulder seam ends at your shoulder bone, not past it.
  • Jacket sleeve: shows ½" of shirt cuff.
  • Jacket length: covers your seat; for formal, to the thumb knuckle.
  • Waistband: no gaping in back when you sit. If it gaps, size down or get it taken in.
  • Break (pant hem): slight fold at the shoe. No puddle.
Online ordering survival
  1. Measure a garment you already love, flat, and compare to the brand's chart.
  2. Read reviews for "runs small/large" — those are the real spec sheet.
  3. Buy two sizes when free returns exist. Return the loser.
  4. Shoes: measure at the end of the day; feet swell. Size to the longer foot.

Everyday Plant Watering Cheat Sheet

Most houseplants die of kindness. Here's how to be kinder, user_name.

Rule one: water on the calendar of the soil, not the calendar on your fridge.
The finger test
  1. Push a finger in up to the second knuckle.
  2. Dry all the way? Water. Damp? Wait.
  3. For big pots, use a wooden chopstick — pull it out like a cake tester.
  4. Water until it runs out the drainage hole, then stop.

No drainage hole? That's a bathtub, not a pot. Water less and empty the saucer.

Over- vs under-watering clues
SymptomUsually means
Yellow, mushy lower leavesToo much water
Crispy brown tipsToo little, or dry air
Wilting despite wet soilRoot rot — too much
Drooping with bone-dry soilToo little
White crust on soilSalt buildup — flush it

Yellow leaves can also mean light, food, or just autumn. One symptom isn't a diagnosis.

Rough watering rhythm
PlantCadence (indoor)
Succulents / cactusEvery 2–4 weeks, bone dry between
Snake plant / ZZEvery 2–3 weeks
Pothos / philodendronWeekly-ish, top inch dry
Ferns / calatheaKeep lightly moist, never soggy

Cooler months = slower growth = less water. Halve it.

Top or bottom watering?
  • Top: fast, flushes salts, mimics rain. Risk: uneven saturation.
  • Bottom: set the pot in a saucer of water for 15–30 min; the soil drinks upward. Great for fuzzy leaves you shouldn't wet.

Either works. Consistency beats technique.

Everyday Canned Food Pantry Cheat Sheet

Cans don't expire the way you think. Here's the shelf exam, user_name.

Best-by ≠ poison-by. Dates on cans are about peak quality, not safety.
How long it actually lasts
ItemQuality window
Low-acid (beans, tuna, soup, veg)2–5 years
High-acid (tomatoes, fruit, pickles)12–18 months
Home-canned (low-acid)1 year, then quality drops

Past the window, flavor fades and texture goes soft. Still safe if the can passes the check below.

The can exam: toss if any of these
  • Bulging ends or sides — pressure inside means bacteria. No exceptions.
  • Leaking or sticky residue on the seam.
  • Deep dents on the side seam or rim. Small dents in the middle of the body are usually fine.
  • Spurting or hissing when you open it.
  • Foul smell or cloudy liquid after opening.
Never taste-test a suspect can. Botulism toxin has no taste. When in doubt, out it goes.
Storage that keeps cans happy
  • Cool, dry, dark. Under 75°F ideally.
  • Off the floor, off concrete, away from the water heater.
  • Don't stack heavy cans on fragile ones.
  • Rotate: new cans to the back, old to the front. Date the lid with a marker.
Cans vs. dried

Dried beans and rice are cheaper per serving and last decades. Cans buy you time and no soaking. The honest answer: keep both, with cans as your "I'm tired tonight" layer.

  • Cans win: speed, no prep, ready emergency food.
  • Dried wins: cost, shelf life, flavor control.
  • Salt note: rinse canned beans to cut sodium ~40%.

Fitted Sheet Folding Cheat Sheet

Hey user_name — no shame in the fitted-sheet struggle. Here's the calm version.

The 4-Step Fold

  1. Find the corners. Hold two adjacent corners of the sheet, right sides together. Let the rest dangle.
  2. Tuck one into the other. Pull the top corner over the bottom one so both elastic corners nest inside each other.
  3. Repeat on the other side. Now you have two corner-bundles. Fold one bundle over the other so all four corners are stacked.
  4. Lay flat and fold. Smooth the sheet into a rectangle, then fold in thirds like a letter. Done.

Pro tip: If you're short on time, fold it into a loose rectangle and shove it in the linen closet. It still works.

Why does this work?

Nesting the corners eliminates the awkward elastic pouches. Once they're all together, the sheet behaves like a flat rectangle.

Red Wine Stain Removal Cheat Sheet

Hey user_name — wine happens. Here's how to make it un-happen.

Act Fast: The Blot & Dilute Method

  1. Blot, don't rub. Use a clean white cloth or paper towel to press down and lift as much wine as possible.
  2. Dilute with cold water. Pour a little cold water on the stain, then blot again. Repeat until the water runs clear.
  3. Apply a cleaning solution. Mix 1 tbsp dish soap, 1 tbsp white vinegar, and 2 cups cold water. Sponge onto the stain, blot, repeat.
  4. Rinse and dry. Sponge with clean water, blot dry, then place a stack of paper towels over the area and weigh it down. Let it air-dry.
What if the stain is already dry?

Soak the area with the cleaning solution for 10–15 minutes, then blot. You may need to repeat a few times. For old stains, a 50/50 mix of hydrogen peroxide and water can help, but test on a hidden spot first.

Avoid: Hot water, which sets the stain, and colored cloths, which can transfer dye.

Daily Care

  • Wash: Use hot water and a stiff brush or chainmail scrubber. Avoid soap unless it's really gunky (modern dish soap won't strip seasoning).
  • Dry immediately: Towel dry, then place on a low burner for a minute to evaporate all moisture.

Scrub with steel wool and a little oil until rust is gone. Wash, dry, and re-season: coat with oil and bake upside down at 450°F for an hour. Repeat a few times.

Three Points, Always

Most home falls start with a stretch, user_name. Don't be the stretch.

The top step and top cap are off-limits. So is the second-to-top of any ladder with a full-height warning printed on it.

Before you climb — a 30-second check

  • Set it within arm's reach of the job — not the job within arm's reach of you.
The angle rule (extension ladders)

Rise 1, run 4. For every 4 ft of height, the base sits 1 ft out. The old test: stand at the feet, arms out — hands should just touch the rung at shoulder height.

For user_name — before you call a plumber, try these steps in order.

First try Boiling water
Then Plunger

Step 1: Boiling Water

Pour a kettle of boiling water down the drain in stages. Wait 30 seconds between pours. Works for grease and soap scum.

Step 2: Plunger (the right way)

Block the overflow hole with a wet rag. Use a cup plunger (not flange) and plunge 15–20 times with force. Hold tight.

Step 3: Baking soda + vinegar

Pour 1/2 cup baking soda, then 1/2 cup vinegar. Cover with a plug for 15 min, then flush with hot water.

Step 4: Drain snake

Feed a hand snake into the drain, crank when you feel resistance, pull out gunk. Wear gloves.

Avoid chemical drain cleaners—they damage pipes and are dangerous if they splash back.

For user_name — flat tire? You've got this. Safety first.

Pull over safely. Turn on hazards, find flat ground, engage parking brake.

  • Step 1 Gather tools: jack, lug wrench, spare, and (if you have it) wheel wedges.
  • Step 2 Loosen lug nuts before jacking. Turn counterclockwise just a quarter turn.
  • Step 3 Place jack under the frame notch near the flat tire. Raise until tire is off the ground.
  • Step 4 Remove lug nuts, pull tire straight off. Put the spare on and hand-tighten nuts in a star pattern.
  • Step 5 Lower the jack, then tighten nuts fully in a star pattern. Check spare pressure soon.
If you're on a slope

Put the car in Park (or 1st gear) and use wheel wedges on the opposite tire. If the slope is steep, call for help—it's not worth the risk.

Spare tires are usually temporary (50 miles max at 50 mph). Get the flat repaired or replaced ASAP.

For user_name — the Four-in-Hand is your friend. Simple, slightly asymmetrical, always works.

Four-in-Hand Knot (Steps)

  1. Drape tie around neck, seam side down. Wide end on your dominant side, about 12 inches lower.
  2. Cross wide end over narrow end.
  3. Bring wide end under and up through the loop around your neck.
  4. Cross wide end in front of the knot.
  5. Pull wide end up through the loop again.
  6. Slide wide end through the front knot loop.
  7. Tighten by pulling wide end down while holding the knot.
Windsor vs. Four-in-Hand

Windsor is wider and more formal—good for spread collars. Four-in-Hand is narrower and casual—works with most collars.

Tie length should hit your belt buckle. If it's too short, the narrow end is too high. Start over with more length.

Yellow leaves, soft stems, gnats, or a sour smell from the soil. Stop for two weeks and let it dry.

Calm hands first. Most kitchen wounds need nothing more than water and a clean cloth.

  1. Wash your hands before you touch anything else.
  2. Rinse the wound under cool running water. No soap inside the cut.
  3. Press with a clean cloth for five minutes. Don't peek.

instances.html:
Chain & Tires, user_name

A quiet chain is a happy chain. Squeaks mean metal rubbing metal, and that wears things down fast.

Chain lubeEvery 160 km
Tire checkWeekly
  1. Wipe the chain with a dry rag before lubing. Dirt plus oil equals grinding paste.
  2. One drop per link. Spin the pedals backwards as you go.
  3. Wait five minutes, then wipe off the excess. Shiny, not wet.
Tire pressure starting points

Road bike: 80–100 psi. Hybrid: 50–70 psi. Mountain: 25–35 psi. Check the sidewall for the real range.

When the chain is done

Pull it away from the front chainring. If you can see a gap of half a tooth or more, replace it. Cheap chain, expensive lesson.

Wet lube for rain, dry lube for dust. Pick one and stick with it in that season.

instances.title: Everyday Button & Zipper Repair Cheat Sheet

instances.html:
Zipper and button fixes that don't need a tailor.

Zipper won't stay closed

Run a graphite pencil along the teeth, or rub with candle wax. The coating adds friction so the slider grips.

Zipper stuck mid-track

Don't yank. Rub a little lip balm or soap on the teeth, then gently work the slider back and forth.

Button fell off

Use a toothpick as a spacer under the button while sewing. It creates a shank so the button sits right over thick fabric. Wrap thread 3–4 times around the shank, knot, and snip.

Prevent future snags

Close zippers before washing. Zip pulls can catch on other clothes and bend teeth.

instances.title: Everyday Toilet Plunging Cheat Sheet
user_requests: how to unclog a toilet without a plumber
toilet overflowing what do i do first
why does my toilet keep clogging
instances.html:
Before you call anyone, try this. Most clogs give up in two minutes.

  1. Turn off the water supply valve behind the toilet. If it's already overflowing, also shut off the main if you can't find the angle stop.
  2. Wait for the bowl to drain. If it won't, use a bucket to remove some water so plunging doesn't splash.
  3. Place the plunger so the rubber cup fully covers the drain hole. Push straight down slowly to seat it, then plunge with quick up-and-down strokes 15–20 times.
  4. On the last stroke, pull up sharply to break the seal and create suction.
  5. If water drains, flush once with the valve still off to test. If it backs up, repeat.

If it still won't drain after three rounds, stop. More plunging can overflow the bowl. Call someone.

instances.title: Everyday Plant Watering Cheat Sheet

how to tell if plant needs water
instances.html:
Forget schedules. Check the soil.

Test before you pour

Stick your finger 2 inches into the soil. If it's damp, wait. If dry, water until it runs out the drainage hole.

Overwatered vs. underwatered

Overwatered: yellowing lower leaves, mushy stems, soil smells sour. Underwatered: crispy brown edges, drooping that doesn't recover after watering, soil pulling from pot sides.

When to water less

Winter, low light, terracotta pots (they wick moisture), and plants with thick leaves like succulents.

When to water more

Summer, bright light, plastic or glazed pots, and thin-leaved tropicals like ferns.

instances.title: Everyday Microwave Cleaning Cheat Sheet

microwave smells bad how to fix
instances.html:
Steam does the scrubbing for you.

  1. Fill a microwave-safe bowl with 1 cup water and 2 tablespoons white vinegar or lemon juice.
  2. Microwave on high for 3–5 minutes until the window steams up.
  3. Leave the door closed for 2 more minutes. Don't open early; the steam needs to loosen the gunk.
  4. Carefully remove the bowl (it's hot). Wipe the inside with a damp cloth. Splatters slide right off.
  5. Remove and wash the turntable and the wave guide cover if it's removable.

For stubborn smells, leave a bowl of baking soda inside overnight.
